cues.text: Local tradition holds that around 1280, a shepherd of Kranenburg , in the Lower Rhine district of Kleve near the modern German-Dutch border, received Holy Communion.
Taken suddenly ill, he found himself unable to swallow the Host and, rather than carry it back to the church, threw it in frustration against a tree in his own garden.
Overcome afterward with remorse, the shepherd confessed what he had done to his parish priest, who came at once to the spot and searched the ground around the tree with him.
The Host could not be found anywhere.
A Crucifix Grown Inside the Wood
Years passed, and the shepherd eventually decided to cut down the same tree.
As it split in two under his axe, a small, perfectly carved wooden crucifix fell to the ground from within the trunk.
Witnesses took this as proof that the Host, though never recovered from the soil, had never truly been lost at all.
A Church for the Miraculous Crucifix
Word of the crucifix that had "grown from a sacred Host" spread quickly from town to town, drawing the attention of the Bishops of Cologne.

In 1408, the citizens of Kranenburg began construction of a church in its honor, completed in 1444—a Gothic building still counted among the most significant examples of that style anywhere along the Lower Rhine.
The Church of St. Peter and Paul in Kranenburg still preserves the relic of the crucifix today, and the town keeps an annual procession in its honor each September 14.
What began as a moment of ordinary human frustration involved a sick shepherd unable to complete a simple act of reverence.
In the memory of the Church, it became a sign that even a Host mishandled and lost to sight could still, in its own time, make itself known again.
